articles.text: Highlands Preschool has enjoyed remarkable consistency with the same beautiful home and only four directors in 70 years of playtime. Their space has all the intangibles preschool age kids desire, a beautiful classroom full of light, a craft room to create, an outdoor space on the Piedmont Community Church campus and even a pet tortoise named Tortellini. In charge of the fun is Angela Livermore, the fourth director of Highlands Preschool who took over in 2024 when Deanna Johnson retired. The lineage of leadership starts with Mary Wood as the first director when Highlands opened in 1955. She passed the torch to her daughter, Joanna Wood, who led the program until Johnson succeeded her started in 1999. The longevity enjoyed in the chief position of the school is a testament to the culture there. Highlands Preschool is run daily by Livermore, Head Teacher Danielle Biondi, Art & Movement Teacher Tracy Herrera and volunteer parents. The space has a magical clubhouse feel and the institution believes wholehearted in learning through play. “You can learn everything through play, kids retain information better that way. We call it sneaky learning,” said Livermore. Danielle Biondi (left), Deanna Johnson, Angela Livermore, and Tracy Herrera at Deanna’s retirement party in 2024.

articles.text: The. City of Piedmont’s new 9-1-1 dispatch center, still under construction, is scheduled to be completed later this year. The new facility replaces an undersized facility that was unable to accommodate modern technology. The new center aims to increase reliability for callers in emergencies. The new dispatch center is the city’s largest public safety investment in decades, costing $3.1 million. The majority of funding for this project came from the American Rescue Plan Act. Construction began in the summer of 2024 with an estimated completion date of winter 2025. The project includes a new independent electrical system, a backup generator, and IT infrastructure for the Police Department. This will ensure that the dispatch center can work through potential outages and environmental emergencies. The next steps for the project include installing servers, cabling, and related equipment in the new Police Department IT room. After the technical groundwork is laid, the center will configure new networking and telecommunications infrastructure and install the next-generation dispatch workstations. The City of Piedmont’s public safety units (police and fire) field more than 13,000 calls each year. The former space in the police department was outdated and not seismically designed. The new center will be a larger, secure, and a technology-ready facility. The new technology being installed will introduce state-ofthe-art call answering equipment that improves cell phone location accuracy and offers real-time, on-screen translation in multiple languages. The new equipment allows dispatchers to continuously monitor automated license plate readers and public safety cameras via large, wall-mounted screens. This improves productivity and reliability within Piedmont’s police department. Concurrent with planned physical space improvements, the City recently augmented dispatch staffing for the first time since 1978. Two new dispatcher positions were added last year, an increase made possible by the passage in March 2024 of Measure F. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Two of my three children have now attended PPS. I can say without hesitation it is the best preschool in Piedmont. Its magic lies not in a fancy curriculum, but in its whole-child approach and its welcoming of parents as collaborators. As a working parent, the co-op model was transformative. Each month, I stepped into the classroom, experiencing my child’s world alongside them. I watched PPS teachers gently navigate conflicts and set up activities that empowered every child. I took those practices home. PPS didn’t just prepare my kids for elementary school; it made me a better parent. Unlike other preschools we attended, where all art was preprinted and uniform, PPS lets kids create from their own imaginations. Children decide how to engage, what to explore, and how to express themselves, supported by expert and caring teachers. The thoughtful curriculum at PPS fulfills the true purpose of preschool, supporting each child’s full potential: social, emotional, and academic. The indoor-outdoor flow is key. The yard is a classroom, too, where children develop motor skills, negotiate turn-taking, and build the social-emotional muscles that matter so much later on. My youngest, who spent two years at PPS, entered kindergarten with an ease I hadn’t seen in her older siblings: she knew how to ask questions and advocate for herself. PPS also quietly builds community for parents. Director Michelle used our parent meetings to bring in child development experts – from child psychologists to nutritionists – whose advice I still share with other parents today. Most importantly, PPS is a place where every child truly belongs. The teachers meet each student exactly where they are, giving them a clear, consistent message: This is your school. You have a place here. That deep sense of belonging stays with them. My daughter, who still plays “school” at home, talks about being a teacher, a seed planted firmly at PPS. In a town that prides itself on educational excellence, Piedmont Play School is one of our greatest assets. It prepares children not just for school, but to become curious, confident, and kind humans. That is the kind of magic a community can’t afford to lose. articles.text: Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan and a resident are pictured at a wildfire-resistant construction planning open house. Piedmont City Council will consider proposed updates to Piedmont’s energy efficiency “Reach Codes” and fire-resistant construction, or “home hardening,” requirements at their regular meeting on Monday, November 17, at 6:00 pm. The proposed changes are part of a larger update to Building and Fire Codes, driven by the State of California, which updates statewide building standards every three years. Cities are required to adopt the new codes and may include local amendments that address community priorities and local conditions. Expanded fire-resistant construction In 2020, the City Council voluntarily designated all of Piedmont as a Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) based on topography, geography, and built environment – steep terrain, mature vegetation, and homes built close together – that make the city susceptible to wildfires. The proposed updates would reaffirm that commitment and ensure that consistent, research-based standards apply across the entire city. Proposed updates would adopt a newly developed State “Wildland-Urban Interface” code, replacing previous Piedmont-specific rules with a comprehensive statewide standard that: • Maintains strict home-hardening requirements for new construction • Expands fire-resistant construction requirements for major renovation projects The choice to continue incorporating these measures into City code – though Piedmont is not required to do so – reflects a clear community value: wildfire resilience matters here. Over the past nine months, extensive community outreach on home hardening found that residents broadly supported keeping Piedmont’s existing protections and expanding them to major renovations. The long-term aim is to make Piedmont’s overall housing stock more wildfire resistant through steady progress over time as new homes are built and existing homes are renovated. Making energy-efficiency Reach Codes easier to achieve Piedmont’s “Reach Codes” are local energy efficiency requirements that go beyond state minimums for certain types of home renovation projects. Proposed updates aim to make these requirements more flexible, easier to meet, and better aligned with current construction costs, while encouraging high-impact measures that advance the City’s climate goals. Proposed updates would: • Add four new compliance options, giving homeowners more ways to meet Reach Code requirements. New items on a “menu” of energy efficiency measures residents can choose from include installing an induction cooktop, a heat pump dryer, or solar panels. • Increase the project value thresholds that trigger Reach Code requirements, reflecting updated construction pricing and reducing impacts on smaller projects. • Strengthen incentives for higher-impact energy upgrades, encouraging actions that will deliver the greatest long-term benefits. If adopted, the updates would take effect on January 1, 2026, in alignment with the statewide Building Standards Code cycle. Open house Objective Design Standards A year and a half in development, Piedmont’s Draft Objective Design Standards aim to create clear, measurable, and enforceable rules governing design for homeowners and developers, with clear and consistent expectations for what new housing in Piedmont will look like. While not dictating specific architectural styles, the draft standards are designed to result in housing consistent with existing housing in the city. State law now requires cities to approve certain new housing proposals, including accessory dwelling units and SB9 applications, based on “objective” standards. Unlike the traditional design review process, these state-mandated “ministerial” permits cannot take into account public comments and do not come to the Planning Commission for approval at a public meeting. When developing the Objective Design Standards, the project team started with Piedmont’s existing Design Review guidelines and looked at how they could be translated into objective, measurable rules. The draft Objective Design Standards were also informed by community feedback received at two open house events, an online survey, and two Planning Commission study sessions. Community members may submit comments by email to kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov or by mail to Kevin Jackson, Planning & Building Director, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. The comment period closes December 7. Learn more about this initiative and see materials and video from previous discussions at piedmont.ca.gov/ObjectiveDesignStandards open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Editor: I’m writing to share my disappointment that the proposed 2026–27 PUSD calendar is essentially a repeat of the past two years and is unchanged despite the district’s efforts to gather community feedback. A total of 455 families participated in the calendar survey, yet the results are nowhere reflected in the outcome. Families even developed and submitted thoughtful alternate calendars, but the proposal again mirrors prior years. Community feedback — and the preferences of Piedmont families — should inform the school calendar, yet under the current structure they hold little weight. The APT-approved calendar passed by only a narrow margin (just above the 50% threshold), suggesting limited consensus even among teachers. Parent groups proposed modest, broadly supported adjustments that would have benefited students, teachers, and families, but they were not considered or implemented. For example: 1. Start school later in August, aligning with instructional pacing and regional family schedules. The request was simply to start 1–3 days later — a small change with big meaning for families wishing to attend summer camps or visit relatives. With the proposed first day on Monday, August 11, PMS and PHS students must return by Thursday, August 6, for walkthroughs on Friday, August 7 — effectively ending summer one week early. 2. Avoid Monday as the first day of school. It creates an unnecessarily long first week for staff and families. Survey feedback favored a mid-week start, yet this was ignored. 3. Shorten Winter Break to a standard two weeks. The proposed schedule extends it to two weeks plus two days, forcing families to find childcare as most working parents return to work on Monday, January 4, while PUSD resumes on January 6. 4 Align with nearby high-performing districts such as Palo Alto and Orinda, which use an 85/95 (or 86/94) semester balance. PUSD’s 87/93 structure remains unnecessarily rigid, especially when “semester classes” make up less than 2% of high school offerings. It’s disappointing to see our district remain tied to an outdated model that no longer reflects the needs of our students, teachers, and families. PUSD can — and should — evolve to better serve the entire Piedmont community. –April Gruber Piedmont parent

articles.text: On December 10, 1975 Articles of Incorporation for the Piedmont Educational Foundation were filed with the Secretary of State. Fifty years later, on November 5, 2025, PEF’s 50th Board and Co-Chairs Rich Thompson and Cameron Wolfe, Jr. hosted a celebration at Piedmont’s Community Hall to commemorate this milestone and to thank PEF’s many heroes. Invitees included current and former Board members, City and School District officials, former employees and Lifetime Donors. Wolfe, an early president of PEF, recounted PEF’s beginnings, noting that the list of signers of the Articles, 12 in all, reads like a list of who was who in Piedmont in the mid-1970s. The person most responsible for the project was Lee Emerson, President of Gilmore Steel and one of the most civic minded leaders in the East Bay. Wolfe was joined by one of the original signers Helen Breck who spoke of the benefits of volunteering. She congratulated all who have worked to make PEF the vibrant organization that it is today. The first meeting of the Board was held in February, 1976, at the home of Emerson, who was elected the first president. The second president was Breck, who also served on the School Board, including a term as president, and on other Boards in Piedmont. Her service with PEF continued from 1975 until her retirement in 1988. In 1971 the second of two decisions by the California Supreme Court entitled Serrano v. Priest had come down. These cases held that funding disparities between school districts violated the California and U. S. Constitutions. In 1978 Proposition 13 was enacted, severely limiting the assessment of property taxes by cities and school districts. The Piedmont City Council turned to a parcel tax, but it was thought not to be permissible by school districts. As f inancial diff iculties mounted the School Board turned to the Ed Foundation. By this time Wolfe’s second special guest, Steffi Mooers had become the third president. Mooers formed a Steering Committee to be responsible for the first of the modern fund-raising campaigns in 1981, co-chaired by Wolfe and Gerry Stahl. Three of these campaigns were to follow. In addition to these campaigns, Mooers described the 1982 founding of Dress Best For Less under the leadership of Wendy Webster Willrich. She also described Piedmont artist Bruce Wolfe’s creation of a logo for PEF. Despite these fundraising efforts, by 1983 the needs of the District reached a staggering $1,000,000. Again the Board turned to Mooers and PEF to fill the gap. Ann Chandler’s recent article described the famous “red thermometer” campaign that ensued. Although that campaign was successful, it was recognized a more stable alternative was needed. It had been determined a parcel tax was legal, and on November 8, 1984, the Board asked the voters to save the District. Yet again it turned to Mooers and PEF. Mooers in turn asked Wolfe and the Steering Committee to conduct a political campaign to obtain a 2/3rd majority, a daunting task given Piedmont’s past history of failed school bond elections. The first step of the campaign was to obtain lists of all registered voters in the 12 Piedmont precincts. Mooers and Wolfe then sent a letter to all Piedmont homes asking people to respond by sending pledges to vote YES. From these pledges, from the Steering Committee’s lists of recent campaign donors, and from dozens of phone calls, a list of YES voters in each precinct was determined. On Election Day Steering Committee members and a legion of helpers made sure that each YES voter made it to the polls. The final result far exceeded the Committee’s hopes: 76% voted YES. At the Celebration, Steering Committee members Breck, Mooers, and Wolfe were present. Also present were two other members, Sue Smegal and Ann Chandler, both of whom, in addition to being on the Steering Committee, provided impressive support to the School District in major ways: Smegal serving as president both of the School Board and of PEF, as well as teaching in the Piedmont Middle School for 10 years; Chandler serving on the PEF Board for many years, publishing countless articles, creating the first Patron and the first All School Directory. Wolfe’s summation of the early history of PEF ended with the passage of the first parcel tax. He noted that by 1987 the success of PEF was out there for all to see. In a survey of the top schools in California, Piedmont High placed 5th out of 50 high schools. The four that topped Piedmont were all magnet schools with competitive admissions. Wolfe concluded the story by noting that the room was full of heroes who have carried on the work of the early volunteers. Along the way the name of PEF was changed to the Piedmont Education Foundation, dropping the original “al.” PEF has been vital to the creation of a top-flight school district. In Wolfe’s view it has changed the character of the City of Piedmont. As the Steering Committee promised voters, property values have soared. The School District has been central to the attraction of a diverse population committed to volunteerism and civic participation. Special thanks to Ann Chandler, whose memory and research provided many of the facts described in this article. To support the continued work of the Piedmont Education Foundation, please visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org/donate.

Wolfe, an early president of PEF, recounted PEF’s beginnings, noting that the list of signers of the Articles, 12 in all, reads like a list of who was who in Piedmont in the mid-1970s. The person most responsible for the project was Lee Emerson, President of Gilmore Steel and one of the most civic minded leaders in the East Bay. Wolfe was joined by one of the original signers Helen Breck who spoke of the benefits of volunteering. She congratulated all who have worked to make PEF the vibrant organization that it is today. The first meeting of the Board was held in February, 1976, at the home of Emerson, who was elected the first president. The second president was Breck, who also served on the School Board, including a term as president, and on other Boards in Piedmont. Her service with PEF continued from 1975 until her retirement in 1988. In 1971 the second of two decisions by the California Supreme Court entitled Serrano v. Priest had come down. These cases held that funding disparities between school districts violated the California and U. S. Constitutions. In 1978 Proposition 13 was enacted, severely limiting the assessment of property taxes by cities and school districts. The Piedmont City Council turned to a parcel tax, but it was thought not to be permissible by school districts. As f inancial diff iculties mounted the School Board turned to the Ed Foundation. By this time Wolfe’s second special guest, Steffi Mooers had become the third president. Mooers formed a Steering Committee to be responsible for the first of the modern fund-raising campaigns in 1981, co-chaired by Wolfe and Gerry Stahl. Three of these campaigns were to follow. In addition to these campaigns, Mooers described the 1982 founding of Dress Best For Less under the leadership of Wendy Webster Willrich. She also described Piedmont artist Bruce Wolfe’s creation of a logo for PEF. Despite these fundraising efforts, by 1983 the needs of the District reached a staggering $1,000,000. Again the Board turned to Mooers and PEF to fill the gap. Ann Chandler’s recent article described the famous “red thermometer” campaign that ensued. Although that campaign was successful, it was recognized a more stable alternative was needed. It had been determined a parcel tax was legal, and on November 8, 1984, the Board asked the voters to save the District. Yet again it turned to Mooers and PEF. Mooers in turn asked Wolfe and the Steering Committee to conduct a political campaign to obtain a 2/3rd majority, a daunting task given Piedmont’s past history of failed school bond elections. The first step of the campaign was to obtain lists of all registered voters in the 12 Piedmont precincts. Mooers and Wolfe then sent a letter to all Piedmont homes asking people to respond by sending pledges to vote YES. From these pledges, from the Steering Committee’s lists of recent campaign donors, and from dozens of phone calls, a list of YES voters in each precinct was determined. On Election Day Steering Committee members and a legion of helpers made sure that each YES voter made it to the polls. The final result far exceeded the Committee’s hopes: 76% voted YES. At the Celebration, Steering Committee members Breck, Mooers, and Wolfe were present. Also present were two other members, Sue Smegal and Ann Chandler, both of whom, in addition to being on the Steering Committee, provided impressive support to the School District in major ways: Smegal serving as president both of the School Board and of PEF, as well as teaching in the Piedmont Middle School for 10 years; Chandler serving on the PEF Board for many years, publishing countless articles, creating the first Patron and the first All School Directory. Wolfe’s summation of the early history of PEF ended with the passage of the first parcel tax. He noted that by 1987 the success of PEF was out there for all to see. In a survey of the top schools in California, Piedmont High placed 5th out of 50 high schools. The four that topped Piedmont were all magnet schools with competitive admissions. Wolfe concluded the story by noting that the room was full of heroes who have carried on the work of the early volunteers. Along the way the name of PEF was changed to the Piedmont Education Foundation, dropping the original “al.” PEF has been vital to the creation of a top-flight school district. In Wolfe’s view it has changed the character of the City of Piedmont. As the Steering Committee promised voters, property values have soared. The School District has been central to the attraction of a diverse population committed to volunteerism and civic participation. articles.text: On November 9, Piedmont student Ivan Tam won the Chess 7th Grade California State Championship in Milpitas. He’s now a back-to-back champion after winning the state’s 2024 tournament for 6th graders. Tam was undefeated in all six matches over the two-day Swiss-system tournament with 280 other middle school chess players from the state. This past year, Tam has spent a lot of effort mastering the Scotch Gambit opening, which he employed successfully in this tournament. “Ivan played very aggressively and used the Scotch Gambit opening. Ivan pretty much dominated the field, none of his matches were competitive,” said his father, Tim Tam. “He had the initiative throughout all his matches. His opponents just tried to defend.” The State Championship tournament coincided with the LA Open in Irvine which attracted some of Tam’s stiffest competition. The LA Open offered kids the chance to compete and earn a title against National Masters and Grandmasters; Tam chose the local tournament instead. For Tam, the State Championship tournament was less about hoisting the trophy at the end and more about getting the chance to bond with teammates from Kings Land Chess (KLC) school. Ivan Tam holds his latest 1st Place Chess trophy after winning the California State Championship for 7th graders. KLC was recently awarded the 2025 FIDE World Gold School award by the International Chess Federation KLC. This honor means KLC is one of the world’s top chess schools and the first institution in the United States to receive this highest international honor. Next month Tam will travel to Spokane, Washington with his KLC chess teammates to compete in the K-12 National Championship.

articles.text: For 142 years, Chabot Space & Science Center has been dedicated to educating learners of all ages about the Universe and our home planet. From early days as a public observatory in downtown Oakland to its current home on Skyline Boulevard, Chabot has served as a hub for discovery, curiosity, and lifelong learning. That mission continues today through the Oakland Space Academy, an initiative designed to help students build career readiness and technical skills for future success in STEM fields. The Academy builds upon the success of Galaxy Explorers, Chabot’s long-standing teen volunteer and education program. Galaxy Explorers play a central role at the Center—guiding visitors through exhibits, leading science demonstrations, and engaging in hands-on inquiry projects. The program provides an opportunity for high school students to explore real-world science topics, from aerodynamics to environmental monitoring, while developing key workforce competencies like teamwork, communication, and critical thinking. This balance of technical training and durable skill-building lays the foundation for the Oakland Space Academy. Students can progress from Galaxy Explorers to more advanced Career Technical Intensives that focus on high-demand STEM skills. These programs go beyond volunteerism, offering applied, project-based experiences that bridge the gap between classroom learning and professional practice. The Academy’s goal is to help young people – and increasingly, adult learners – gain both confidence and capability in science, engineering, and technology. “I’m most excited about creating an informal learning environment where students can develop both creativity and engineering skills,” says Ben Tagami, Engineering Lead at the Oakland Space Academy. “There’s something valuable about stepping away from traditional classroom structure and giving students time and space to explore and tinker.” That philosophy of exploration is at the heart of Chabot’s approach. The Academy offers a range of technical and science intensives designed to engage students through doing. Upcoming workshops include an Astrophotography Workshop, where participants learn to capture images of the night sky, and a Drone Challenge, where students aged 15–25 will design, build, and code their own object-tracking drones. These experiences emphasize problem-solving, collaboration, and applied technical skills—qualities essential in today’s evolving workforce. The Academy’s programs are also informed by strong local roots. By anchoring STEM education in Oakland, Chabot aims to make space- and science-related careers visible and accessible to local students. Participants have opportunities to work with Chabot’s staff, collaborate with peers, and connect their learning to real-world applications. In an era when much learning happens within rigid classroom structures, the Oakland Space Academy demonstrates the value of learning outside the classroom. Through hands-on exploration, mentorship, and skill development, it empowers students to see themselves not just as learners, but as emerging scientists, engineers, and innovators. As Chabot continues its 142- year legacy of curiosity and education, the Oakland Space Academy represents a forward-looking chapter. One where the next generation of Oakland’s thinkers and makers can discover their place among the stars. Baringer’s GPS watch, which normally tells sunrise and sunset time, merely showed “--:--” in Antarctica, where the sun menacingly circles 24 hours a day. On the way to High Camp the pitch of the climb increased dramatically to nearly 45 degrees. The climbers latched onto fixed ropes and slowly chewed their crampons into the glacier for a grueling ascent. The path tapered off to 25 degrees as they made it to High Camp at 12,400 feet. But for Baringer, a perpetual hiker, the “rest” part was optional. On the day off he set his sights on Mt. Shinn, the 3rd highest peak on Antarctica at 15,289 feet, visible from High Camp. After strategic nudging, their mountaineering guide Vern Tejas, a legend among mountain climbers, agreed to take Baringer and fellow climber Steve Plain, up Mt. Shinn. Thinking the peak of Shinn was right above, Baringer left his ice axe there too. Some moments later it became apparent that a knife edge of ice and snow required an ice axe. Tejas gave his axe to Baringer, and they continued. Shortly after, Baringer fell and using the axe tried to self-arrest, but slid downhill a few yards in a frightful moment. On top of the southernmost part of the world, Bill Baringer stood tall at the summit of 16,070- foot Mt. Vinson. Having completed the summit with time to spare, the team got to spend 45 minutes at the top. Baringer took some photos of friend Steve Plain, who was attempting to break the record for time taken to conquer all seven summits. It was Plain’s first of the seven summits. He later went on to complete all seven in 117 days to become the world record holder. Baringer continued to accomplish his goals and acquire friendships along the way. Fellow hiker Chris Newton said, “Bill will be very hard to forget. He was an exemplary team player and a great example of how training, passion and commitment can conquer age.” With this summit, Baringer had climbed to the top of the highest peak on four continents. After trekking to the end of the world, sunny Piedmont awaited his tales of conquest. NEXT WEEK: Part 5 of Bill Baringer’s quest to climb the highest peak on each continent. In May 2018 he attempted an ascent of 20,308-foot Mt. Denali in Alaska. Climbers ascended Mt. Vinson with a white-on-white view of the placid sky, snow and glacial expanse. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team, seeded No. 2, started off its Division 7 North Coast Section playoffs in a big way, dominating No. 7 St. Patrick 49-7 in Vallejo on Friday, November 14. With the victory, the Highlanders are now set to host No. 3 Willits this Friday, November 21 at Witter It is the second straight year for PHS to reach the semis. Friday’s game against Willits will be the first time Piedmont has hosted an NCS Semifinal since 2014, when the No. 2 Highlanders fell to eventual NCS champion No. 3 Justin Siena. Piedmont will be favored in Friday’s game against Willits. With a win, the school could make history by reaching the NCS Championship game. According to available online records, it appears PHS has not made a championship appearance since its storied 1976 title-winning program. Since the 1976 Hall of Fame team, Piedmont High has reached the semifinals four times, including in 1981, 2014, 2016, and 2024. Now, the championship game is truly feeling in reach. “It’s looming. We have a great opportunity to be there. Considering what we lost from last year and the group that graduated, we have a group of scrappy guys who really put things together,” coach Jordan Seiden said. It was a big night for senior running back and linebacker Xavier Henderson who recorded 215 rushing yards on 15 carries for two touchdowns, averaging an eye-popping 14.3 yards per carry. Henderson, he had to miss a couple of games this season due to injury, making the performance that much more special to him. “Just coming off an injury was tough. I had to fight back for my spot, nothing is given and it’s always the next man up. The team trusts me enough to run the ball, and I trust my offensive line all the way,” Henderson said. Cash Panico also had a big night with three touchdown receptions on four receptions for 51 yards. Panico has shown skill in snatching the ball at its high point. He did so for his second touchdown, leaping in a one-onone situation to get the ball. “Most of them, we set up in a run, then we check to coach. Jimmy makes the throw and I got up to get it. I always try to highpoint the ball where the defender can’t get it. A lot of defenders I go up against aren’t too tall, so I try to take advantage,” Panico said. Beam’s death made national news after the former Laney College and Skyline HS coach became a star in the Netflix film, Last Chance U, in 2020. But he was much more than a reality TV personality. For countless athletes and coaches, Beam was a mentor, friend, father-figure, and a community pillar. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis season came to an end over the past week. The Highlanders lost 5-2 to No. 5 Northgate in the first round of the Division 1 North Coast Section Team Tournament. For the first time Piedmont was the No. 12 seed. The match was pkayed at home at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Tuesday, November 11. PHS also had three players in the Division 2 NCS Individual Tournament on Monday, November 17. Ella Ruthven competed in the singles bracket, losing 6-4, 6-2 to Justin Siena’s Lyla Hogan. In the doubles bracket was Samantha Huynh and Emma Chan, losing 6-1, 6-2 to No. 1 seed Jane McDermott and Ann McDermott of Marin Academy. Despite the losses, Piedmont ends the season as this year’s league champion in the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division. Also Chan and Huynh won the team’s first-ever WACC Doubles title. “It was a great season. We were League Champions and played a lot of really good tennis. In the NCS Individual yesterday, Ella Ruthven lost in first round to Lila Hogan, a really tough player for Justin Sienna. Sam and Emma ran into the McDermott sisters, who were the tournament’s top seed from Marin Academy,” coach Jim Landes said. Against Northgate, the Highlanders won at No. 3 singles and No. 2 doubles. Faith Chin won her singles match in straight sets, 6-4, 6-2. At doubles, Inara Mehta and Chiara Silvio dominated their match 6-3, 6-1. At singles, Ella Ruthven lost 6-3, 6-3 at the No. 1 spot, while Kate Jumper lost 6-4, 6-0 at No. 2. Arianna Kortum took her No. 4 singles match to three sets, but lost 3-6, 6-2, 6-2. Huynh and Chan also kept things competitive at the No. 1 doubles spot, losing in a narrow three-set battle by scores of 6-4, 4-6, 10-4. Piedmont’s No. 3 doubles team of Leela Sivakumar and Ella Thomasson also fell in a heated three-set battle, 6-4, 1-6, 6-2. The Highlanders end their season with a 13-9 overall record. They will watch key starters depart with the Class of 2026, including Huynh, Jumper, Kortum, Mehta, Maddie Tran, and Lila Rosen. Looking ahead to next year, Piedmont will find leadership from multi-year starters like Chan and Chin, while people like Ruthven, Silvio, Thomasson, and Sivakumar bring more starters back into the fold. Ruthven could resume the No. 1 singles role, while Chan can lead the doubles roster or fit into singles when needed. Chin also provides a strong returner to Landes’ singles order. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team gets back into action on Saturday, November 29 at Gateway School in San Francisco for its first official opening game of the 2025-26 season. The Highlanders return after going 15-16 and falling 75-70 to St. Patrick in the Division 4 North Coast Section championship game, marking the school’s second consecutive championship game appearance. The Highlanders watched their leading scorer, Ravi Silverberg, graduate with the Class of 2025, but bring back an experienced group with six seniors, five juniors, and just one sophomore. Four returning players will lead the way; Dillon Casey, P.J. Brayer, Lucian Fang Ring, and Beach Lorin. “Returners are so important in high school athletics, bringing back six seniors is huge. I think this year is our deepest group of guards that I’ve ever had,” said coach Ben Spencer. Casey enters his third year as a starter and will likely eclipse the 1,000-career point mark early in the season. “Dillon will be the best player on the floor most nights. He’s at 925 points and is really close to breaking 1,000. He’s been starting at us for three years and I can’t say enough about what he does. He handles the ball 99 percent of the time, gets us into our offense, is a great off-ball defender, and is a great team leader,” Spencer said. Brayer is another captain and was an every-game starter last season. He’ll provide presence on the boards, while he’s shown a propensity to knock down a 3-pointer. “P.J. cleans up the boards, he’s an animal. He’s skilled and fast, get to the basket, and he also can shoot. We’ll be able to spread out the floor with him,” Spencer said. Fang Ring is another player who proved to be dependable from beyond the arc. He gained minutes as a starter last year during his sophomore season, and will have an increased role as a junior. “He’s really improved his ball-handling. There were a couple of games last year where Dillon got in foul trouble and Ravi was hurt, so we had Lucian play the one. articles.text: Remembering Jack Nelson, Soren Dixon through the game they loved Soren Dixon and Jack Nelson, two remarkable young men whose love for lacrosse and strong leadership on and off the field, will continue to inspire and support rising student-athletes in the Bay Area. Approaching the one year anniversary of their tragic passing, Oakland Lacrosse Club is honored to announce the creation of the Purple One ScholSharing their love of lacrosse Soren and Jack were standout four-year varsity players at Piedmont High School, helping lead their team to league titles in 2021, 2022, and 2023. In their senior season, they advanced to the 2023 Division 2 NCS Final as the No. 3 seed, falling just short in double overtime to top-seeded Tamalpais. According to teammate Noah Lindenbaum, Soren and Jack raised the bar for the Piedmont Lacrosse Program: “In our years as upperclassmen, what had once seemed a dominant sport at Piedmont was beginning to lose steam. Fewer people seemed interested in lacrosse, and enrollment on the team reached a low. Soren and Jack weren’t satisfied with that. They raised the standard of play by emphasizing teamwork and dedication. Doing so turned what seemed to be a small team with dwindling numbers into a powerhouse in our division, worthy of winning a championship.” Off the field, their leadership and generosity shone even brighter. Both volunteered as youth coaches, mentoring younger players and sharing their passion for the game. Their athleticism and spirit extended far beyond lacrosse. Jack had a lifelong passion for sports and was a member of multiple travel lacrosse and soccer teams. At Piedmont High, he was a rare three-sport varsity athlete—football, soccer, and lacrosse—where his strength, speed, and leadership made him a force of nature. As captain of the varsity lacrosse team, he played virtually every minute of every game, leading Piedmont to multiple championships and ultimately earning the title of Piedmont High School Athlete of the Year. Soren was a match for Jack’s spirit and athleticism, also playing three varsity sports and leaving a lasting impact on the team. A fierce competitor and dedicated teammate, Soren started all four years on the varsity lacrosse team and was selected captain his junior and senior seasons. His teammates were drawn to his energy, passion, and unwavering commitment, qualities that made him a leader both on the field and among his inseparable crew of friends. articles.text: Guest conductor Jane Glover The San Francisco Symphony will present George Frideric Handel’s Messiah, a musical meditation on Christ’s birth, life, and resurrection, on December 5 and 6. Guest conductor Jane Glover leads the symphony and chorus in this classic holiday favorite. Glover is a fellow of the Royal College of Music and was the artistic director of opera at the Royal Academy of Music between 2009 and 2016. In December 2013, she became the third woman ever to conduct at the Metropolitan Opera of New York, leading Mozart’s The Magic Flute. Performers include Susanna Phillips as soprano, Jennifer Johnson Cano as mezzo-soprano, Josh Lovell as tenor, and Will Liverman as baritone. Davies Symphony Hall will be decked out for the holidays during these performances, filled with lit evergreen trees, wreaths and garlands. The hall’s lobby bar will feature festive winter cocktails, including a Gingerbread Old Fashioned, limited-time sparkling wine and holiday-themed desserts throughout December. The Friday and Saturday performances both begin at 7:30 p.m. A preconcert talk by San Francisco Symphony’s resident lecturer Laura Stanfield Prichard will be presented onstage at 6:30 p.m. before both performances. The preconcert talk is free to all ticketholders. Tickets are on sale at https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2025-26/HANDEL-MESSIAH or call the box office at (415) 864-6000 to purchase tickets. ®

articles.text: The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco unveiled a major reinstallation of Native American art at the de Young museum, highlighting the deep ties between Indigenous peoples and the Bay Area and beyond. The new presentation spans more than a millennium of artistic expression in North, South and Central America, developed with a group of Native America co-curators. The refreshed Arts of Indigenous America galleries at de Young feature both ancestral works and contemporary pieces, including new acquisitions and specially commissioned artworks. The four-gallery suite features two newly developed spaces for Native American art, alongside updated galleries of Ancestral Maya works and mural fragments from Teotihuacan. Native American art has been central to the Fine Arts Museums’ collections since the museum’s founding in 1895, but this reinstallation represents a transformational approach to curation and community engagement. Indigenous scholars and community advisors participated from the project’s inception, shaping the selection of works and interpretive strategies, said Hillary Olcott, Curator of Arts of the Americas at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “We consult with communities of origin to determine how to care for the artworks and cultural items in the collection, and which are appropriate to share with the public,”Olcott said in a press release. “The curatorial team has chosen to frame these items through neither an art historical nor an anthropological lens, but rather a blend of the two. We have also opted for a multivocal interpretative framework instead of a single curatorial perspective. Our hope is that this will bring a liveliness to the galleries and will re-center people within the stories of this art.” “The reconceived Arts of Indigenous America galleries embody our ongoing commitment to building lasting collaborative partnerships with Indigenous communities,” added Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums. “This spirit of collaboration has had a transformational effect in our newly reinstalled galleries, where visitors may find their understanding of Native art expanded.” Visit https://www.famsf.org/ to learn more and plan your visit. pages.text: 16 16 Wednesday, November 19, 2025 Arts & Entertainment SF Symphony to perform Handel’s Messiah Dec. 5 & 6 de Young Museum’s reimagined Native American art galleries now on display By Allyson Aleksey The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco unveiled a major reinstallation of Native American art at the de Young museum, highlighting the deep ties between Indigenous peoples and the Bay Area and beyond. The new presentation spans more than a millennium of artistic expression in North, South and Central America, developed with a group of Native America co-curators. The refreshed Arts of Indigenous America galleries at de Young feature both ancestral works and contemporary pieces, including new acquisitions and specially commissioned artworks. The four-gallery suite features two newly developed spaces for Native American art, alongside updated galleries of Ancestral Maya works and mural fragments from Teotihuacan. Native American art has been central to the Fine Arts Museums’ collections since the museum’s founding in 1895, but this reinstallation represents a transformational approach to curation and community engagement. Indigenous scholars and community advisors participated from the project’s inception, shaping the selection of works and interpretive strategies, said Hillary Olcott, Curator of Arts of the Americas at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “We consult with communities of origin to determine how to care for the artworks and cultural items in the collection, and which are appropriate to share with the public,”Olcott said in a press release. “The curatorial team has chosen to frame these items through neither an art historical nor an anthropological lens, but rather a blend of the two. We have also opted for a multivocal interpretative framework instead of a single curatorial perspective. Our hope is that this will bring a liveliness to the galleries and will re-center people within the stories of this art.” “The reconceived Arts of Indigenous America galleries embody our ongoing commitment to building lasting collaborative partnerships with Indigenous communities,” added Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums. “This spirit of collaboration has had a transformational effect in our newly reinstalled galleries, where visitors may find their understanding of Native art expanded.” Visit https://www.famsf.org/ to learn more and plan your visit. Guest conductor Jane Glover By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Symphony will present George Frideric Handel’s Messiah, a musical meditation on Christ’s birth, life, and resurrection, on December 5 and 6. Guest conductor Jane Glover leads the symphony and chorus in this classic holiday favorite. Glover is a fellow of the Royal College of Music and was the artistic director of opera at the Royal Academy of Music between 2009 and 2016. In December 2013, she became the third woman ever to conduct at the Metropolitan Opera of New York, leading Mozart’s The Magic Flute. Performers include Susanna Phillips as soprano, Jennifer Johnson Cano as mezzo-soprano, Josh Lovell as tenor, and Will Liverman as baritone. Davies Symphony Hall will be decked out for the holidays during these performances, filled with lit evergreen trees, wreaths and garlands. The hall’s lobby bar will feature festive winter cocktails, including a Gingerbread Old Fashioned, limited-time sparkling wine and holiday-themed desserts throughout December. The Friday and Saturday performances both begin at 7:30 p.m. A preconcert talk by San Francisco Symphony’s resident lecturer Laura Stanfield Prichard will be presented onstage at 6:30 p.m. before both performances. The preconcert talk is free to all ticketholders. articles.text: Visit Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside beginning November 22 to see the 16-acre estate lit up for holidays. Every year in November, Filoli’s decorating team installs and decorates 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate adobe for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreates the original holiday placement that is indicative of Agnes and William Bourn, the house’s first residents. More original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene, one of her favorites, is displayed in the study. Winter-themed cocktails and treats are available for purchase throughout the holiday season at Filoli’s Quail Cafe and Chalet bars. This year, guests can upgrade their tickets for an exclusive reception in Filoli’s grand ballroom. Tickets include a glass of Moet champagne, or uninterrupted pours of Dom Perignon for an extra fee. Non-alcoholic options are available. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively in the daylight. Daytime admission gains you access to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The estate is open until 9 p.m. beginning November 22. Last tickets for Filoli’s holiday festivities are sold at the door at 7 p.m. To learn more about “Holidays at Filoli” and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/holiday-lights/. articles.text: Rami Bar-Niv The piano concert in our Piedmont Center for the Arts Sunday afternoon was inspiring from beginning to end. The pianist was Rami Bar-Niv. His biography states that he is one of Israel’s most acclaimed and sought after pianists. He deserves this acclaim. Perhaps I am stating the obvious: good musicians always play well. Their performances are always inspired. Throughout the concert, a backdrop sign on the wall was emblazoned with the words: “considering the nature of inspiration”. This is the stated philosophy of artist Michael Stehr and his words were prophetic. It is my habit to arrive early and listen to the musicians warming up. Rami Bar-Niv has an easy-going manner. But as soon as he sits down at the piano, he is ready to play. In reality, he doesn’t need to warm up. In every aspect, he is serious about his art. It is quite obvious that music comes first. Bar-Niv’s accomplishments are all-encompassing. He has a commanding tone and technique which he modulates in a most artistic way. He knows how to emphasize a phrase and how to offer the appropriate contrasts. As was the case for the great pianists in the past, the music speaks for itself, and the performer presents it to the audience in the most appropriate manner. There is no need for gimmicks; lofty, artistic playing speaks for itself. As the concert progressed, it became obvious that we were listening to an outstanding pianist. Every composition was interpreted with intelligence. The speed of each piece, which we musicians refer to as tempo, was in keeping with the composer’s intentions. There was no mindless speed, which seems to be the main ingredient of the young generation. Sunday’s program was playing on the grand scale. The program itself was well thought out and well balanced. A few well-chosen words by the pianist were very appropriate. And then he was ready to go. The program opened with the Bach-Busoni adagio from the Toccata in C Major. Bar-Niv’s artistry is such that he can create the sound of a grand organ while he plays the piano. It was a supersmooth and expressive legato, hinting at outstanding singing. Second on the program was the Mozart Sonata in F major. The mood changed. So did the performer’s persona. He literally became a classic-period musician. No sooner had the Mozart ended then the pianist introduced the composer JJ Hollingsworth. The San Francisco composer was present and sitting in the front row. Her composition: “Cobalt Moon and Stars“ from the Glass Suite was all too brief. The pianist explained that there were certain very special piano techniques. Interesting? Absolutely. He concluded the first half of the program with his own composition entitled “Rhapsody in Blue and White“ which is based on three Hebrew songs. Nothing beats a composer playing his own music, and it was performed with an expansive and virtuoso approach. What is amazing is that the playing was so expressive in the simplest way. After a brief intermission, the audience was treated to a very characteristic performance of Polonaise in A flat major by Chopin and his introspective and expressive Nocturne in C-sharp minor, a work of Chopin’s youth. The pianist explained the nature of a Polonaise, a processional dance of noble character. It must be stately. It is, after all, of noble character and nobility never rushes. The program concluded with Bar-Niv’s arrangement of Rhapsody in Blue by Gershwin. This excellent arrangement featured some mind-boggling finger work. Throughout the program we experienced expansive playing on the grand scale. All of the ingredients were present. Despite the bright acoustics of the hall, the soloist was able to evoke sensitive dynamics. I had a delightful conversation with Bar-Niv following the concert. He told me that he is 80 years old. It’s hard to believe. He has perfectly timed humor in addition to a youthful manner of playing which gives no hint to his age. How fortunate the Piedmont audience was on Sunday.

articles.text: Dog Man: The Musical, based on Dav Pilkey’s best-selling children’s book series, will make its East Bay debut at the Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts on January 3. The production is scheduled for three performances: Saturday, January 3, 2026, at 11 a.m. and 4 p.m., and Sunday, January 4, 2026, at 1 p.m. Pilkey, author and illustrator of the children’s popular series books Dog Man, Captain Underpants, and Cat Kid Comic Club, called the musical adaption “the perfect mash-up of memorable music, humor, and love.” The touring production brings Dog Man’s adventures to life, starring a crime-fighting hero with the head of a dog and the body of a police officer as he battles Flippy the cyborg fish, an army of Beasty Buildings, and the villainous Petey the cat. The story also follows young creators George and Harold as they rush to finish their show before lunchtime. O r ig i n a l ly p r e m ie r i ng off-Broadway in 2019 and returning in 2023, Dog Man: The Musical has been celebrated by critics for its humor and energy. The cast features Mundo Ballejos as Harold, Nick Manna as Dog Man, Sadie Jayne Kennedy as Li’l Petey, Troi Lennoxx Gaines as George, Anthony Rodriguez as Petey, and Diamond Destiny as Flippy. Swings include Zack Abbey, Jeremiah Rosado, and Emerese Noel. The musical includes book and lyrics by Emmy Award winner Kevin Del Aguila and music by Brad Alexander, with original direction and choreography by Jen Wineman. The creative team also includes scenic designer Timothy R. Mackabee, costume designer Heidi Leigh Hanson, lighting designer David Lander, sound designer Emma Wilk, orchestrator Lloyd Kikoler, and music director Miriam Daly. Tickets, priced from $25 to $68, are now available at hjkarts. com. Originally premiering off-Broadway in 2019, Dog Man: The Musical has been celebrated by critics for its humor, energy, and broad appeal to audiences of all ages.

articles.text: It’s an interesting experience to approach a film with one set of expectations and realize, as the story evolves, that it is something else entirely. That’s the case with Mr. Holmes. Going in I assumed that the setting would be London, during those nascent years of the 20th century, not long after the end of WWI. Mr. Holmes is at the top of his deductive game and often takes intricate cases with subtle clues to be cleverly unraveled. Buttressing my assumption is the fact that Ian McKellen, a gifted character actor, is portraying Holmes, sans deerstalker cap and oversized Meerschaum pipe (something Watson added), but in all ways a perfectly cast Holmes. But Mr. Holmes is a decidedly different movie. Based on the novel A Slight Trick of the Mind, by Mitch Cullin, the narrative is set in 1947. Sherlock Holmes, now in his 90s, is living on his bucolic Sussex farm. He has been retired for some 30 years and has used this time to raise bees and study botany. He lives a solitary life, with the exception of his housekeeper, Mrs. Munro (Laura Linney), and her precocious 10-yearold son, Roger (Milo Parker). As is soon made evident, Mr. Hattie Morahan and Ian McKellen in Mr. Holmes Holmes is a penetrating character study of a man once renowned, thanks to the embellished writings of his friend and case collaborator, Dr. John H. Watson, who wrote what Holmes refers to as “penny dreadfuls” about their exploits. He has retreated from his former life and is now confronted with the harsh realities of aging – his once keen mind going sideways, his powers of observation, always the fulcrum of his detection, growing increasingly elusive. Holmes is gradually becoming a man who has outlived the person he once cherished: his former self. His daily frustration with his decline, compounded by regret for certain choices from his past, has made him taciturn and even a bit desperate. articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Zootopia Zootopia is not your typical animated talking animals movie; rather, Disney created a family-friendly buddy cop comedy with a raft of subtle messages and teachable moments. The film is set in a world where predator and prey identities have been abolished, hence Zootopia (utopia). The story focuses on Judy Hopp (Ginnifer Goodwin), the first metropolitan bunny cop ever hired. She’s a perky go-getter. Determined to prove herself. But officer Hopps, on her first day on the force, to her surprise, confronts some discouraging prejudices. Given her size, and given some thickheaded assumptions, officer Hopps is assigned parking ticket duty by her Cape Buffalo police chief, Bogo (Idris Elba). But then Judy learns that a family man Otter has disappeared and his wife, Mrs. Otter, is frantic, and appeals to Judy to find him. Judy rises to the challenge and so bets her career that she can. The problem is that in order to track Mr. Otter down, she will have to partner up with slick and sly fox, Nick Wilde (Jason Bateman), which forces her to rethink her assumptions about foxes in general. The team’s search for the missing Mr. O. takes the pair in unexpected directions, while encountering the most extraordinary cast of characters, examples being an adorable lamb; a mafiatype polar bear; and a wonderful sloth who works for the Department of Motor Vehicles, which means extremely slow service and long, exasperating lines. Judy and Nick must also unravel an unanticipated conspiracy, one that tests their teamwork, and tucks nicely into that thread of prejudice that stitches the narrative together at every turn. But there are also moments of silly slapstick, exciting chases, all while taking them into fascinating enclaves of Zootopia known as Tundra Town, Sahara Square, and little Rodentia. For all of the film’s asides, and not too subtle references to Disney’s Frozen, the most significant are the scenes, however nuanced, that touch on racism in everyday Zootopian life. Hopps, for example, makes the point that “cute” is a word used only by bunnies and considered offensive if used by other denizens of Zootopia. What Disney points out, often with the lightest of touches, is that we are all tempted to prejudge one another, even by the most benign Judy Hopps. However, when Judy is confronted by her blind spots regarding Zootopians, she willingly steps up and apologizes to those she has offended and promises to do better. All of this takes place in the context of a fun, exiting movie with lots of laughs and energetic, fastpaced animation that pays close attention to detail and texture. Zootopia, Disney animation. Directed by Byron Howard, Rich Moore. With voices of Ginnifer Goodwin, Jason Bateman, Idris Elba. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG. Streaming on Disney+/Apple tv/ Prime/HBO MAX/Roku.

The joyful yips, comical play bows, and the inevitable chaos can result in owners roaring with laughter. But did you know that encouraging your puppy to engage in play, thereby building social skills, is actually essential for healthy development? Similar to people, puppies must also learn social skills at a young age to live successful lifestyles. Confidence is part of it, yes, but so is learning to read the physical body language of other dogs. An adult dog with good social skills has the ability to engage in play without fear, but also understands when another dog is signaling they are not interested or even fearful. This well-socialized adult dog will also be able to set their own boundaries without starting fights. All of these skills are learned in a critical socialization age for puppies between 3 and 14 weeks old, and much of this is learned with their littermates. The joyful yips, comical play bows, and the inevitable chaos can result in owners roaring with laughter. But did you know that encouraging your puppy to engage in play, thereby building social skills, is actually essential for healthy development? Similar to people, puppies must also learn social skills at a young age to live successful lifestyles. Confidence is part of it, yes, but so is learning to read the physical body language of other dogs. An adult dog with good social skills has the ability to engage in play without fear, but also understands when another dog is signaling they are not interested or even fearful. This well-socialized adult dog will also be able to set their own boundaries without starting fights. All of these skills are learned in a critical socialization age for puppies between 3 and 14 weeks old, and much of this is learned with their littermates. What happens if a puppy is not well socialized? They can become fearful, which is the number one cause of aggression. Not every nervous dog presents an immediate bite risk, but the most common reason people and dogs are bitten is because they fail to read a dog’s clear signs that they are afraid and saying “no thank you” to being touched. Having a multitude of social interactions, the majority of them being positive, will give your puppy the confidence to know when a situation is safe as well as the ability to comfortably set their own boundaries. So how does a new pet parent find ways to socialize their dog? A good way to start is by joining a puppy training class. A competent trainer who understands that socialization is equally as important as obedience will provide time during their puppy class for play. This will simultaneously increase your dog’s social skills and provide much-needed brain breaks. An example of a class structured this way is the one taught by Mike Wombacher. During his classes, puppies and owners learn new skills, as well as getting significant play time. Owners receive feedback from the trainer about puppy socialization and play to build their understanding of healthy canine interactions. And of course, your pup will have the time of their lives testing out their budding social skills in play. By prioritizing socialization, you will set your puppy up for a successful life of wail wagging and joy. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland. articles.text: The 2nd annual Piedmont Adult Recreation Expo was held on November 16, from 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. at the Veterans Memorial Building. The event featured 25 recreation providers and was attended by approximately 200 people. The event was co-chaired by Recreation Commission members Dick Carter and Lisa Gardner. Their subcommittee reviewed existing activities throughout Piedmont and the general Bay Area. They conducted a community survey that reached nearly 500 responses. It identified a lack of knowledge about existing opportunities as the primary reason more people weren’t participating. “A lot of our adults and seniors are not all tech savvy, so a lot of them weren’t aware of things that were being offered online. As a result of the survey, we made a recommendation that we do an in-person event, which we called the Expo,” said Gardner. The Expo offered a chance to learn about available programs and discuss details with the organizers, including Piedmont Adult School. “The things the survey found were that people want to be involved. They just didn’t know how… We looked at what we had offering in Piedmont and pulled them all together in one house, in one day,” said Gardner The Expo provided a place for adults to learn about the activities that interested them. “We know that loneliness and isolation are serious problems for older adults. [It was a compelling motivation],” added Carter. The Expo was made possible through the efforts of Piedmont volunteers and in collaboration with the Recreation Department, the Piedmont Adult School, and the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts. articles.text: Picture my client, a wildly successful entrepreneur whose innovation and drive propelled him into the top half-percent. His life was one of luxury: yachts, private planes, global travel, and a beautiful mansion on one of the most distinguished streets in the East Bay. I’ve known him my entire life. To me, he was strong, charismatic, and absolutely a force to be reckoned with. But as time went on, subtle changes began to surface. The brightness in his eyes dulled. His sharpness softened. His longtime companion, overwhelmed by what she believed was controlling and irritable behavior, eventually had to move on. She didn’t realize he wasn’t being difficult — he was changing. Slipping. Losing control. When I visited him, I found a man I barely recognized — surrounded by a lifetime of belongings and memories, growing thinner, sadder, and more frustrated by the day. This wasn’t just the stress of a move. This was the unraveling of independence, identity, and the confidence he once carried with ease. Sadly, this wasn’t the first time I’d witnessed such a decline. More recently, I’ve spent the last decade helping another dear friend — a once vibrant traveler, respected and admired, supported for years by a loving husband who has since passed. I’ve watched as she, too, has begun to slowly unravel with age. Strength turning to fear. Confidence slipping into confusion. Even the simplest decisions become overwhelming. Is it dementia? Is it aging? Or is it the disorienting experience of life suddenly spinning beyond one’s control? It’s hard to know. But one truth remains: no one should have to navigate this alone. These experiences have reinforced something profoundly important: we must plan ahead. For ourselves, for our aging parents, and for the people we love — long before the need becomes urgent, and before a crisis makes the decisions for us. It’s not just about choosing a community with pretty surroundings or a full social calendar. It’s about understanding the depth of care, the consistency of support, and the human connection that actually exists. Ask: Will someone check in daily? Will they notice changes? His longtime companion, overwhelmed by what she believed was controlling and irritable behavior, eventually had to move on. She didn’t realize he wasn’t being difficult — he was changing. Slipping. Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I have an iMac that I bought in 2023. My son keeps telling me to upgrade to the new operating system, Tahoe. Is there any reason to do that? I have not upgraded anything since I bought it. He said something about easier organization with the new one, as I am trying to write my memoir. Jayne, Oakland Dear Jayne: Although I often caution clients to wait for the .2 release of a new operating system (e.g. OS Tahoe 26.2), I have found Tahoe to be very stable, even though at this writing we are on OS Tahoe 26.1. The reasons for keeping your operating system up to date mostly have to do with security but sometimes upgrades contain exciting new features. One misconception is that the updates that happen automatically will keep things current. But those are updates, not upgrades, and only apply to the operating system that is already on your computer. For instance, if you have Sequoia installed on your Mac, the updates that happen automatically only pertain to Sequoia. So, an update applies to your current operating system and an upgrade is a new one. The actual operating system upgrade will only happen when you initiate it. Another reason to update your OS, is that in the eventual act of getting a new computer, keeping up with the changes will prevent you from feeling like a stranger in a strange land, as often the interface changes with each upgrade. Now, since you are writing your memoir, I think that Tahoe (OS 26) could be very helpful in helping you organize your files. Let me list a few of my favorite features. 1. CUSTOMIZE FOLDERS: Many years ago, there was some third party software that allowed you to color code your folders, not just apply colored dots next to the folder title. Tahoe allows for a real customization of each folder. If you want all your folders to be a different color, you can do that in System Settings/Appearance. There you can change all your folders to a different color than the default blue. But what I like to do is to change each folder or group of folders to a different color. To do this, right-click (or hold the control key and click) on a folder and choose the Customize Folder option in the contextual menu. You can even apply and emoji or symbol. This is very helpful if you have many folders and feel like you are wading through an ever-expanding sea of blue to find the ones you need. 2. FOLDER ICON CHANGES: Speaking of folders, I know many times we have folders that are empty. Now you can tell by looking whether a folder has items inside. You will see a bit of virtual paper sticking out. This makes it much easier to clean out unwanted empty folders without having to open each one. 3. SYSTEM THEMES: In System Settings/Appearance, you can even change the theme of your whole interface. You can change the highlight color, the way the dock looks, whether it’s more or less transparent, among other things. 4. HOLD ASSIST: Many of us use our computers to make and receive phone calls. In the phone app, when you are waiting to speak to a person, you can activate Hold Assist. Your mac will let you know when an agent is on the line and inform the person on the other end that you will be right with them. 5. LIVE TR ANSLATION: This is perhaps my favorite. Facetime now supports live translation. If you are talking to someone who speaks another language, FaceTime can display captions in your language. This feature utilizes Apple Intelligence and you must have an Apple silicon Mac (all of the computers with M1-M5 chips). These are just a handful of the new features on OS Tahoe, with new ones being added with each update. To initiate an operating system upgrade, go to: System Settings/General/Software Update. Before doing any major upgrade make sure you have a current back up to Time Machine, and that any third-party software that you use is compatible. You can usually find that information on the developer’s website. Also, make sure your Mac is new enough to handle the upgrade. For Tahoe, Apple provides this site to check if your machine is compatible: https://support.apple. com/en-us/122867. articles.text: Daley Mae Sarver Humphries, a beloved wife, mother, grandmother, cousin and friend, passed away at home in Piedmont surrounded by family and so much love on Sunday, November 2, 2025, shortly after her 77th birthday. Daley is survived by her husband, Mike Humphries; daughters Alisa Sarver Latvala (Rich) and Amy Sarver Engler (Jeremy); step-children, Steven Humphries (Amy) and Mary Jane Rogers (Chris); and grandchildren, Thomas, Henry, Maia, Sydney, Olivia, Eva, Aubrey, and Ella. Born on October 13, 1948, in Oakland, she was the daughter of Anne and Marvin Blankstein. She attended Crocker Highlands Elementary School, and graduated from Oakland High. She was a 3rd generation alumni of UC Berkeley where she earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in History. Earlier in her career she managed dental offices before completing her Society for Human Resources Management (SHRM) certification. She spent many years working for Levi Strauss & Company in Human Resources before completing her professional career at Abbott Laboratories, after which she retired to be a full time Grandma, helping to raise her grandchildren. She was an incredibly engaged and nurturing grandmother who helped with everything from caring for her grandchildren as infants, to driving them to all of their activities and showering them with love, always. Her grandchildren adored their “Maea”. Daley loved many things in life, but nothing compared to the love she had for her daughters, grandchildren, husband and family. Daley was a mom to all and a devoted partner to Mikey, her heartthrob. Together they created a warm and loving home that became the hub for lively dinner parties with an abundance of shared laughter, sleepovers, holiday gatherings and a myriad of celebrations. Daley created a positive, warm, accepting environment where people felt comfortable being their authentic selves. Her home became a place of comfort to many. Daley was most happy when surrounded by her family and friends, and made a point to tell her loved ones just how much she loved, cherished, and appreciated them, always finishing a conversation by saying, “I love you,” Daley Mae Humphries died on November 2, 2025. She was 77. and then, “I love you more.” She enjoyed cooking, reading, music, happy hours, game days, family gatherings, holidays and celebrations, vacations in Hawaii and traveling internationally with Mike and their lifelong friends. As a child and younger adult, she enjoyed time spent in Tahoe skiing, waterskiing, and being outdoors. She was an avid Cal fan, known for displaying her Go Bears spirit at Cal games and throughout the many years spent camping at the Lair of the Bear. She was the best mother to her daughters - unconditionally loving, empathetic, caring and encouraging. She was known as the fun and cool mom, always welcoming and hosting many in her home with open arms. She was an animal lover through and through – many compared her to Snow White. With a magnetic personality and vibrant sense of humor, Daley was always up for a good time, often being the last one to leave a party. Goodbyes took hours. She is known for her kindness, compassion, vibrance, sense of humor, smile, laughter, welcoming nature, and pristine skin. She will be remembered for sharing her light, love, sparkle, wit and warmth with all who knew her. A celebration of life and memorial service will be held on Sunday, November 23, at 11 a.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. The family requests that attendees wear something sparkly or colorful in honor of her vibrant and radiant personality and her love of sparkles. In lieu of flowers, please consider donating to your local animal shelter or food bank in honor of Daley.

Friend and teammate Nate Carter Fredericks shared: “Jack and Soren are two of the most positive and driven people I’ve ever played with. They always brought light and laughter to every situation, even when things were tough. Their energy and determination were contagious. You could feel it in every huddle and play.” In memory of Jack and Soren, friends and family have gifted over $130,000 to Oakland Lacrosse Club. These contributions will carry forward the values these young men exemplified—teamwork, perseverance, and joy in the game—through the Purple One Scholarship and the Helmets Rising Initiative, our new endeavor to expand boys high school lacrosse in Oakland Unified School District. Purple One Scholarship Jack and Soren’s bond was rooted in their shared love of sports and the joy they found in playing together. The name of the scholarship, “Purple One,” comes from a play the Piedmont team ran, one that always ended with Soren passing to Jack for the goal. Even when opposing teams had seen it before and tried to stop it, it still worked. The play captured everything about their friendship and teamwork: trust, connection, and the pure joy of competing side by side. Teammate Henry Brayer believes that the Purple One scholarship “an amazing way to honor their legacy while encouraging others to adopt the qualities that made Soren and Jack such amazing teammates and people.” Launching Spring 2026, this annual scholarship will award two $2,500 scholarships to graduating senior boys’ players from Oakland Lacrosse Club. The scholarship will support the educational pursuits of club participants as they continue their academic journeys. The Purple One Scholarship celebrates the qualities that defined Jack and Soren on and off the field—qualities Brayer, a teammate for eight years through youth and high school lacrosse, will always appreciate: “Jack was a fearless leader that prioritized the well being of his teammates. Soren was a very selfless player. He chased assists rather than goals and was the first guy to praise his teammates.” Each year, two graduating senior boys from Oakland Lacrosse Club will be selected who embody the same spirit that made Jack and Soren such beloved teammates. These Oakland players will be recognized for their leadership, the quiet kind that lifts others up and strengthens the whole team. The selection committee will be looking for student-athletes who have heart and hustle, the ones who show up to every practice ready to work hard and inspire those around them. Moreover, recipients will be chosen not for their statistics or records, but for how they show up for their team, school, and community. Like Soren and Jack, awardees will be great teammates, the kind who earn respect not through words, but through actions, effort, and unwavering positivity. And they’ll be enthusiastic ambassadors of the game, sharing their love of lacrosse with others and helping to grow access and opportunity for the next generation. Through Purple One, Jack and Soren’s legacy lives on in every player who leads with compassion, plays with joy, and builds community through the game they loved. The scholarship recipients will be chosen by a panel that includes members of Soren’s and Jack’s families, Piedmont teammates Nate Fredericks, Henry Brayer, and Noah Lindenbaum, and a representative from Oakland Lacrosse. Recipients will be recognized at the Oakland Athletic League (OAL) Championships, celebrating their achievements both on and off the field. Teammate Noah Lindenbaum sees the scholarships as a passing of the torch, an inheritance of a legacy of excellence, from Soren and Jack: “For lacrosse, this means playing hard, practicing harder, emphasizing teamwork, and being grateful for every second they’re on the field. Off the field, this means emphasizing academic achievement, serving as a role model for your peers, and living a life that fulfills your passion. Soren and Jack were irreplaceable, and I know they’d be
